analysis.one_liner: Imposes a small tax on stock and futures trades to make Wall Street pay for its own bailout.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 34 Democratic cosponsors during the 2008 financial crisis, the 0.25% tax on stock and futures trades never got a hearing or a vote in the Ways and Means Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Days after the Bush Administration proposed a $700 billion bailout of Wall Street during the 2008 financial crisis, this bill would have imposed a 0.25% tax on trades of stocks, options, futures, and other financial instruments — about 25 cents per $100 traded. The exchanges would collect it, and the money — an estimated $150 billion a year — would go to the general treasury. The United States had a similar stock transfer tax from 1914 to 1966, and the United Kingdom still has one at 0.5%.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers. The bill's stated purpose was to raise roughly $150 billion a year to offset the $700 billion the Bush Administration was asking Congress to spend bailing out Wall Street's "illiquid" assets, with all revenue going to the general treasury rather than to any industry [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers funding the Wall Street bailout

how_it_helps.text: It would have raised an estimated $150 billion a year — roughly a fifth of the $700 billion bailout — from the financial industry that the bailout was designed to protect, with all revenue going to the general treasury rather than to any industry [S3].
It would have spread the cost of rescuing Wall Street onto Wall Street itself, using a tax the bill's findings described as having a negligible impact on the average investor [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Financial firms. The tax would be collected by the exchanges and trading venues where securities, futures, and other derivatives change hands, and its cost would land on the banks, hedge funds, and high-volume traders who buy and sell them. A small share could trickle into slightly higher costs for everyday investors, though the bill itself argued the impact on the average investor would be negligible [S3].

drawbacks.text: A transactions tax is paid by the trading venue, but some of the cost could be passed through to ordinary investors in the form of higher trading costs, and critics generally argue such taxes can push trading to overseas markets, reducing the revenue collected [S3].

Even at the bill's own $150 billion a year estimate, the tax would not by itself have covered the $700 billion bailout, so taxpayers would still have borne most of the cost while markets absorbed a new levy during a crisis [S3].
The bill contained no provision directing how the new revenue would be used beyond deposit in the general treasury, so there was no guarantee it would offset the bailout specifically [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade was straightforward: make the industry being rescued help pay for its own rescue. A 0.25% levy is small per trade, and the United States had an even smaller one for half a century without apparent harm, so the main risk — some cost passing to small investors and some trading moving offshore — is real but modest relative to $150 billion a year in revenue. The bill's biggest weakness is design, not concept: the revenue went to the general treasury with no earmark, so Congress could have spent it on anything.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 26, 2008, during the congressional debate over the $700 billion Wall Street bailout, with 34 Democratic cosponsors [S3][S4].
It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
The bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wall Street. Financial firms that would have paid the 0.25% transaction tax never faced it, and the cost of the $700 billion bailout stayed with taxpayers and the federal debt instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wall Street trading firms avoided the tax

for.name: Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 34 original cosponsors, all Democrats, within the House

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote — letting it die when the Congress ended

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the two-year Congress

against.name: Financial industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed new taxes on financial transactions during the 2008 crisis; the securities and banking industry generally fought such levies, and no Republican cosponsored the bill

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — 34 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans — and the bill died in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have levied a 0.25% tax on every covered securities and commodities trade, collected by the trading venue. In 2008 its members were also the beneficiaries of the $700 billion bailout the tax was meant to offset, so the industry's interest in the bill ran directly against taxpayers'.
Under the bill, the exchanges and futures markets where trades occur would be legally responsible for collecting and paying the 0.25% tax, giving them a direct financial stake in stopping it.
